title: Session Guarantees
description: Understand monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read-your-writes, and writes-follow-reads, with implementation via sticky routing and version vectors.

segments.text: Eventual consistency sounds reasonable until your user updates their profile picture and the page refreshes to show the old one. They click refresh again: new picture. Refresh again: old picture. The user thinks your site is broken. Session guarantees prevent exactly this class of problem without requiring strong consistency for everyone.

Read-your-writes is the most critical session guarantee. After a user writes data, their subsequent reads must reflect that write. It doesn't mean every user sees the write immediately, just the user who made it. Implementation: route all of that user's reads to the replica that received their write, or track the write's version and only serve reads from replicas at that version or later.

Monotonic reads guarantee that once you've seen a value at version 5, you'll never see it at version 4 again. Without this, a user might see the latest product price on one page load, then an older price on the next because they hit a different replica. This is confusing and can cause real business problems like checkout price mismatches.

Monotonic writes guarantee that a user's writes are applied in the order they were issued. If a user changes their email from alice at old to alice at new, no replica should apply the second write before the first. Without this, some replicas might end up with the old email as the final value. Causal ordering of writes within a session.
segments.thought_prompt: How is monotonic writes different from linearizability? What does it NOT guarantee?

segments.text: Writes-follow-reads is the subtlest guarantee. If a user reads a value and then makes a write based on what they read, the write is guaranteed to be ordered after the read. Example: user reads a forum post, then replies. The reply must be causally ordered after the post, not appear before it on any replica.

The simplest implementation: sticky sessions. Route all requests from a given user to the same replica using consistent hashing on the session ID or user ID. If you always read from the same replica you wrote to, you automatically get read-your-writes and monotonic reads. AWS ALB supports sticky sessions with cookies.

Sticky sessions have problems. If the pinned replica goes down, the session loses its guarantees until it re-establishes on another replica. Load can become uneven because some replicas serve more active users. And in serverless or highly elastic environments, pinning to specific instances is architecturally painful.

Version vectors are the robust alternative. Each write carries a vector of logical timestamps, one per replica. When a client reads, it remembers the version vector. On the next read, it sends the vector, and the system only serves data from a replica whose vector is greater than or equal to the client's. The client can hit any replica that meets the version requirement.
segments.thought_prompt: Version vectors grow linearly with the number of replicas. How would you handle a system with thousands of replicas?

segments.text: In practice, most teams combine approaches. Use sticky routing as the primary mechanism. Fall back to version-aware routing when the sticky replica is unavailable. DynamoDB offers strongly consistent reads as an option per request. Cosmos DB lets you choose from five consistency levels per operation. The flexibility to tune per query is the modern answer.

Session guarantees occupy the sweet spot between eventual and strong consistency. They give users a consistent experience without the performance cost of global consistency. Most users don't need to see every other user's writes immediately. They just need to see their own. That insight saves you enormous architectural complexity.
